annotation.title_clean: Robot taxation as a fiscal policy instrument for sustainable employment: A scoping review with implications for developing economies
annotation.title_en: Robot taxation as a fiscal policy instrument for sustainable employment: A scoping review with implications for developing economies
named_instruments_referenced: EU Civil Law Rules on Robotics 2017
annotation.summary_en: Scoping review (Arksey & O'Malley) by University of KwaZulu-Natal authors on robot taxation as a fiscal response to automation-driven job displacement and lost income tax revenue. It argues that South Africa and other developing economies should consider a robot tax to fund retraining and correct tax biases that favour capital over labour.
key_provisions_or_claims: Automation reduces personal income tax revenue and increases fiscal pressure
A robot tax could offset lost revenue and fund retraining, reskilling and upskilling of displaced workers
Current tax law (e.g., SA Income Tax Act s11D, s12C) favours capital investment over labour
Analysis is framed by Smith's maxims of taxation, Christensen's disruptive innovation theory and Pigouvian tax theory
Implementation challenges include defining a robot and identifying the taxpayer; international coordination (e.g., Oberson's imputed salary model) is needed
